Test Doubles
Just like in movies where stunt doubles are used for dangerous scenes instead of the main actors, when we write tests to eliminate unwanted side effects, we use doubles.
We use test doubles when a functionality requires collaboration from other entities, and those entities are very complex, forcing us to create a multitude of tests or producing side effects like saving data to a database or calling external services.
Test doubles behave exactly as the real entity should, but only regarding the behavior we’re testing. Everything else isn’t important to us. They’re most commonly used in unit tests, but they can perfectly be used in other types of tests (integration or e2e).
In the world of testing, there are two main schools of thought, basically related to TDD:
•
Solitary tests, where the unit is much more aligned with the programming language’s unit (classes, functions, modules, etc.). Test doubles are heavily used between different language units to control behaviors.
•
Sociable tests, where the unit is the behavior being tested, and the use of test doubles is greatly limited. Lately, many people advocate for creating lots of integration tests and having a trophy instead of a test pyramid (with the base in unit tests).
My opinion leans much more toward sociable tests, but without falling into what I believe is a mistake: more integration tests than unit tests. If you’re looking for a broader explanation, here it is: unit tests.
When to Use a Test Double?
I usually do TDD, so when I realize a functionality exceeds the boundaries of the entity I’m building (e.g., it has no relation to the layer I’m creating), I create an interface and generate a test double for it.
This allows me to build from the most abstract entities (top-down design) without paying much attention to the details of the more specific ones. Basically, it’s applying the Dependency Inversion principle from SOLID.
For example, in a REST application, I could build the controller by creating a test double for the service that handles my app’s logic. This way, I can test that the controller does what’s expected of it, bridging the view world (JSON, HTTP, etc.) with my business logic world.
I can then create a test for my controller:
•
That can spin up an HTTP server.
•
That can respond to GET, POST, PUT requests or whatever on the URL I decide.
•
That returns an object in whatever format (JSON, HTML, XML) when I pass it specific parameters or a body in the request I make.
The implementation details of my service, at the time of creating the controller, are somewhat irrelevant, making it a great candidate to be replaced by a test double. Basically, this decision is marking a separation between two worlds: the infrastructure world related to HTTP and my business logic/domain world. I’m creating layers in my design; it’s applying the dependency inversion principle; it’s the root of Hexagonal Architecture.
Then, in this approach, we realize that test doubles allow me to define the boundaries of my layers. And they give us another great opportunity: defining what our next layer should do. With certain input parameters, our test double returns a predefined response. This fact represents a contract between the test double and what the real code must do.
Each assumption made in my test doubles should represent a test for my real service, so by applying the chain rule, we’ll have everything created with tests at different levels.
If our domain services need to create some side effect, like writing to a database, for example. There’s another opportunity to apply dependency inversion; we shouldn’t base ourselves on details of how the database works or have our entities, objects, or functions depend on it. Let’s create another interface and another test double to work on those details later (last responsible moment).
Types of Test Doubles
Dummy: These are used to fulfill a method’s signature, but our functionality doesn’t actually depend on them; they’re not used or are only used to retrieve some attribute they contain. The simplest example is when testing a functionality in a specific scenario where there are unused parameters; we can pass nulls there if our language allows it ().
Fakes: These are simpler alternative implementations of the real object, but not ready for production because they don’t meet some non-functional requirement of our system—for example, an in-memory database. Fakes are very useful for testing infrastructure; a controller will need an HTTP service to check that it’s actually listening, but it doesn’t necessarily have to be a full server—we can use a library that works but loads faster.
Stubs: These are entities with preprogrammed responses to certain questions. In our previous example, if the service must return an object with certain values R when we pass it input A, we’d create a stub that does exactly that: if we pass input A, it returns R. Stubs are very useful for replacing code that returns results without having created that code yet. For example, if we’re doing hexagonal, we can use stubs to replace the repositories (from hexagonal) that we use.
Spies: Spies are proxies over real entities or stubs to verify that they were called with certain parameters. Spies can be useful when it’s not easy to replace a real implementation, but we want to check that it’s called in a certain way.
Mocks: These are similar to stubs, but they allow verifying that they were called with the correct parameters in the test. In a way, mocks verify the behavior that our service under test has with respect to its collaborators. Mocks allow us to be strict about the behavior we expect to occur with respect to our test doubles—how they’ll be called and with what parameters. I think they’re great for checking command execution where I don’t care about the return response, void methods.
